lead: Anti-lock braking (ABS) and traction control (TCS) both keep a tyre near the slip where it grips best. ABS does this by building, holding and releasing brake pressure many times a second. TCS does it by reducing engine torque or braking a spinning drive wheel. The same wheel speed sensors and hydraulic modulator serve both. You meet them on cars, two-wheelers and trucks, especially in rain, on gravel and during panic stops.
prereq: You need: wheel speed sensing from Unit 3, the hydraulic and electrical supply from Unit 1, and the pressure modulator idea used again in ESP.

sections.h3: Slip ratio and the friction peak

blocks.text: Let v be the vehicle's forward speed in m/s, ω the wheel's angular speed in rad/s, and r the wheel radius in m. The wheel's contact patch tries to move at ωr. Slip ratio is λ = (v − ωr)/v. λ is dimensionless. Free rolling gives ωr = v, so λ = 0. A locked wheel has ω = 0, so λ = 1. Under braking, slip rises from 0 towards 1.

blocks.where: v is vehicle forward speed (m/s); ω is wheel angular speed (rad/s); r is wheel radius (m); λ is slip ratio (dimensionless).

blocks.text: The tyre's friction coefficient μ depends on λ. μ is the ratio of friction force to normal load, so it has no unit. A typical dry-asphalt curve rises steeply, peaks near λ = 0.15 and then falls as the wheel locks. Wet road has a lower peak. Figure 1 shows both curves. If λ is held near the peak, the tyre gives more braking force than a locked tyre. That is the whole aim of ABS. The controller does not need the exact peak; it watches wheel speed, estimates λ, and keeps it in a narrow band, often about 0.10 to 0.20.
For a drive wheel, wheel spin makes ωr larger than v. The same formula gives a negative λ. TCS works on the magnitude of that drive slip and limits it near the friction peak.

sections.h3: ABS hardware and the pressure cycle

blocks.text: Each wheel carries a toothed ring and a wheel speed sensor. An inductive sensor makes an AC voltage whose frequency follows tooth passage; a Hall sensor gives a clean square wave. The ABS electronic control unit (ECU) compares the four wheel speeds. A wheel dropping faster than the others is close to locking.

The hydraulic modulator sits between the master cylinder and each brake. For each wheel it has an inlet valve, an outlet valve and a low-pressure accumulator; a return pump sends fluid back to the master cylinder. The ECU runs three phases:

items: Build: inlet valve open, outlet valve closed; brake pressure rises.
Hold: both valves closed; pressure is trapped.
Release: inlet closed, outlet open; fluid escapes to the accumulator and the return pump runs.

blocks.text: The ECU repeats build-hold-release about 5 to 15 times per second. This is fast enough to hold λ near the peak but slow enough for the hydraulics. Electronic brake distribution (EBD) uses the same hardware to apportion rear brake force and reduce rear lock before ABS acts. On loose gravel or fresh snow, a locked wheel can push a wedge of material and stop sooner. ABS prevents that wedge, so the stop can be longer. That is not a fault; it is the price of steering control.

TCS uses the same wheel speed sensors. It compares a driven wheel with a non-driven wheel or with the vehicle speed. If a drive wheel spins, λ is negative and its magnitude rises past the grip peak. TCS then acts in this order, as needed:

items: Reduce throttle opening through the electronic throttle, or cut fuel and spark on older systems.
Retard ignition timing to cut engine torque quickly.
Brake the spinning wheel through the ABS modulator.

blocks.text: Braking one spinning wheel also helps an open differential. An open differential gives equal torque to both wheels, so a wheel on ice limits the torque to the gripped wheel. Braking the spinning wheel creates a reaction torque; the differential then sends more torque to the wheel with grip. This is the differential-brake idea. Some systems also reduce the throttle limit for a short time after the spin ends, so the tyre does not break away again. TCS and ESP share sensors and brakes, but TCS controls drive slip while ESP controls yaw.

examples.question: A car travels at v = 20 m/s. Its wheel radius is r = 0.30 m. (a) The wheel turns at ω = 60 rad/s. Compute the slip ratio λ and state whether ABS holds pressure if its target band is 0.10 ≤ λ ≤ 0.20. (b) Under hard braking the wheel drops to ω = 40 rad/s. Compute λ and state the ABS action.
steps: Slip ratio: λ = (20 − 18) / 20 = 2 / 20 = 0.10. This lies in the target band, so ABS holds pressure.
λ = (20 − 12) / 20 = 8 / 20 = 0.40. This is past the peak, so ABS releases pressure until slip returns near 0.15.
examples.answer: λ = 0.10 at 60 rad/s (ABS holds), and λ = 0.40 at 40 rad/s (ABS releases).
examples.check:
v = 20.0
r = 0.30
w1 = 60.0
w2 = 40.0
slip1 = (v - w1 * r) / v
slip2 = (v - w2 * r) / v
print(slip1)
print(slip2)

traps: Slip ratio uses vehicle forward speed v as the reference; it is dimensionless, so do not add m/s.
λ = 0 is free rolling and λ = 1 is a locked wheel. For a spinning drive wheel the formula gives a negative λ; TCS uses the magnitude.
ABS can lengthen a stop on loose gravel or fresh snow because a locked wheel builds a material wedge.
Build opens the inlet valve; release opens the outlet valve and runs the return pump. Do not swap them.
The pressure cycle rate is about 5 to 15 per second (Hz), not per minute.

quiz.q: Define slip ratio and state the units of each symbol.
quiz.a: λ = (v − ωr)/v; v is in m/s, ω in rad/s, r in m, and λ is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Name the three ABS pressure phases and the valve state in each.
quiz.a: Build: inlet open, outlet closed. Hold: both closed. Release: inlet closed, outlet open.

quiz.q: Why does ABS keep slip near 0.15 instead of locking the wheel?
quiz.a: The friction curve peaks near 0.15, so holding near the peak gives more braking force than a locked wheel and still allows steering.

quiz.q: How does braking a spinning wheel help an open differential?
quiz.a: Braking the spinning wheel creates reaction torque. The open differential then sends more torque to the wheel with grip instead of letting the spinning wheel take it all.

quiz.q: A car at v = 25 m/s has r = 0.32 m and ω = 70 rad/s. Compute λ.
A drive wheel at v = 20 m/s, r = 0.30 m spins at ω = 120 rad/s. Compute λ and say whether TCS should cut torque.
quiz.a: ωr = 120 × 0.30 = 36 m/s. λ = (20 − 36)/20 = −0.8. The magnitude 0.8 is far past the grip peak, so TCS should cut torque.

quiz.q: ABS on loose gravel may lengthen the stop. Explain why, and why a driver may still prefer ABS.
quiz.a: A locked wheel on gravel pushes a wedge of material that adds braking force. ABS keeps the wheel rolling, so no wedge forms and the stop is longer. The driver still gains steering control and less wheel lock, which often matters more than a shorter stop.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production ABS uses model-based slip estimation and sensor fusion rather than a single wheel-speed threshold. Electric vehicles blend regenerative braking with hydraulic ABS, which makes pressure control harder because motor torque must fall as the wheel recovers. Functional safety work follows ISO 26262. Search for slip ratio observer, regenerative braking ABS blending and traction control differential brake.
